items.title: Archaic Greece
items.description: City-states, colonies, tyrants and the alphabet.

items.title: Classical Greece
items.description: From Salamis to the death of Alexander.

items.title: The Fifty Years
items.description: Athens grows from leader of an alliance into an empire.

items.title: Greco-Persian Wars
items.description: Persia against the Greek cities, first in Ionia and then in Greece itself.

items.title: Battle of Marathon
items.description: Athenians and Plataeans beat the first Persian landing.

items.title: Xerxes’ invasion
items.description: A great army and fleet cross the Hellespont.

items.title: Battle of Salamis
items.description: The Greek fleet wins in the narrow strait.

items.title: Delian League founded
items.description: Greek cities pool ships and money against Persia, with Athens in the lead.

items.title: Helot revolt in Messenia
items.description: The helots rise after the earthquake; Sparta asks Athens for help, then sends it home.

items.title: Ephialtes’ reforms
items.description: The Areopagus loses most of its powers to the Council, the Assembly and the courts.

items.title: Long Walls built
items.description: Walls join Athens to its harbour at Piraeus.

items.title: Athenian expedition to Egypt
items.description: A fleet sent to help an Egyptian revolt is destroyed.

items.title: League treasury moves to Athens
items.description: The money moves from Delos to the Acropolis, and the alliance becomes an empire.

items.title: Pericles’ citizenship law
items.description: Citizenship needs an Athenian mother as well as father.

items.title: Peace of Callias
items.description: A peace with Persia, if it happened; ancient writers disagree.

items.title: Pay for jurors begins
items.description: Poorer citizens can afford to sit on juries.

items.title: Parthenon built
items.description: A marble temple to Athena, paid for from the empire’s tribute.

items.title: Thurii founded
items.description: A panhellenic colony in southern Italy.

items.title: Megarian decree
items.description: Megarian merchants are shut out of Athens’ harbours and markets.

items.title: Peloponnesian War
items.description: Athens and its empire against Sparta and the Peloponnesian League.

items.title: Archidamian War
items.description: Sparta invades Attica each summer; Athens raids the coast.

items.title: Sicilian Expedition
items.description: The greatest fleet Athens ever sent out is lost at Syracuse.

items.title: Pericles’ funeral oration
items.description: A speech over the first year’s dead, praising Athens and its way of life.

items.title: Plague of Athens
items.description: Crowded behind the walls, perhaps a quarter of the people die.

items.title: Herms mutilated
items.description: In one night the stone herms of Athens are defaced, just before the fleet sails.

items.title: Rule of the Four Hundred
items.description: An oligarchic coup replaces the democracy for a few months.

items.title: Trial of the generals
items.description: Six victorious generals are executed together for not rescuing the sailors.

items.title: The Thirty take power
items.description: A pro-Spartan oligarchy rules for about eight months.

items.title: Democracy restored
items.description: Thrasybulus leads exiles back from Phyle; an amnesty follows.

items.title: Theban attack on Plataea
items.description: Plataean victory. About 300 Thebans got in by night; most were killed or taken.

excerpt.text: In March 431 BC a Theban force slipped into Plataea at night; the Plataeans rallied and killed or captured them.

items.title: Potidaea surrenders
items.description: Athenian victory. After a siege of more than two years.

items.title: Phormio's victories
items.description: Athenian victory. 20 Athenian ships against 47, then 77.

excerpt.text: With only twenty ships, Phormio beat a Peloponnesian fleet of forty-seven, then won again off Naupactus.

items.title: Mytilene surrenders
items.description: Athenian victory. The Assembly voted to kill every man, then changed its mind the next day.

excerpt.text: A second trireme, sent a day later, arrived just in time to stop the killing at Mytilene.

items.title: Plataea falls
items.description: Spartan and Theban victory. The defenders who were left were put to death.

items.title: Pylos and Sphacteria
items.description: Athenian victory. 292 Spartans surrendered, 120 of them full citizens.

excerpt.text: The surrender of 292 Spartans on Sphacteria shocked Greece; Spartans were not expected to give up.

items.title: Delium
items.description: Boeotian victory. Socrates was among the hoplites in the retreat.

excerpt.text: At Delium the Boeotians routed the Athenians; Socrates was among the hoplites who fell back in good order.

items.title: Amphipolis taken
items.description: Spartan victory. Thucydides, then a general, came too late and was exiled for twenty years.

excerpt.text: The historian Thucydides, then a general, arrived too late to save Amphipolis and was exiled.

items.title: Battle of Amphipolis
items.description: Spartan victory. Cleon and Brasidas were both killed, which opened the way to peace.

excerpt.text: Cleon and Brasidas, the leading voices for war on each side, were both killed at Amphipolis.

items.title: Mantinea
items.description: Spartan victory. The largest land battle of the war.

excerpt.text: Mantinea was the largest land battle of the war, and restored Sparta's name after Sphacteria.

items.title: Siege of Melos
items.description: Athenian victory. The men were killed; the women and children were enslaved.

excerpt.text: After the siege, the Athenians killed the men of Melos and sold the women and children as slaves.

items.title: First battle at Syracuse
items.description: Athenian victory. Nicias won, but did not begin the siege until spring.

items.title: Battle in the Great Harbour
items.description: Syracusan victory. The Athenian fleet was trapped and beaten.

excerpt.text: Beaten in the Great Harbour, the Athenians could no longer escape by sea.

items.title: Assinarus
items.description: Syracusan victory. Nicias surrendered; the prisoners were sent to the quarries.

excerpt.text: The prisoners were held in the stone quarries of Syracuse, where many died.

items.title: Cynossema
items.description: Athenian victory. The first Athenian naval victory after Sicily.

items.title: Cyzicus
items.description: Athenian victory. The Spartan fleet was destroyed and its admiral Mindarus killed.

excerpt.text: Sparta's message home after Cyzicus: “Ships lost. Mindarus dead. Men starving. Don't know what to do.”

items.title: Notium
items.description: Spartan victory. Alcibiades was away; he never led the fleet again.

items.title: Arginusae
items.description: Athenian victory. Six of the winning generals were executed for leaving sailors to drown.

excerpt.text: Despite the victory, the Assembly executed six generals for failing to rescue sailors in a storm.

items.title: Aegospotami
items.description: Spartan victory. Lysander caught the fleet on the beach; about 170 ships were lost.

excerpt.text: Lysander caught the Athenian fleet drawn up on the beach at Aegospotami and took almost all of it.

items.title: Athens surrenders
items.description: Spartan victory. The Long Walls were pulled down and the fleet cut to twelve ships.

excerpt.text: Athens surrendered in 404 BC; its Long Walls were pulled down and its fleet was limited to twelve ships.

items.title: March of the Ten Thousand
items.description: Greek mercenaries fight their way home from the heart of Persia.

items.title: Trial of Socrates
items.description: Condemned for impiety and corrupting the young.

items.title: First catapults
items.description: Engineers working for Dionysius of Syracuse.

items.title: The King’s Peace
items.description: Persia dictates terms to the quarrelling Greek cities.

items.title: Battle of Leuctra
items.description: Thebes breaks Sparta’s army and its reputation.

items.title: Messene founded
items.description: The helots are freed; Sparta loses half its land.

items.title: Battle of Mantinea (362)
items.description: Thebes wins, but Epaminondas is killed.

items.title: Social War
items.description: Athens’ allies break away.

items.title: Third Sacred War
items.description: Phocis seizes the sanctuary at Delphi.

items.title: Philip’s pike phalanx
items.description: Infantry with pikes five or six metres long.

items.title: Battle of Chaeronea
items.description: Philip beats Athens and Thebes; his son Alexander leads the cavalry.

items.title: Lamian War
items.description: Athens and its allies rise against Macedon and lose.

items.title: Macedonian garrison at Munychia
items.description: Citizenship is limited to men worth 2,000 drachmas.

items.title: Silver strike at Laurion
items.description: A rich vein pays for the fleet that wins at Salamis.

items.title: Athenian silver “owls”
items.description: Coins stamped with Athena’s owl become a common currency around the Aegean.

items.title: Trireme fleets
items.description: A warship with 170 oarsmen in three banks.

items.title: Hoplite phalanx
items.description: Citizens in bronze armour fighting shoulder to shoulder.

items.title: Piraeus laid out on a grid
items.description: Planned by Hippodamus of Miletus.

items.title: Cult of Asclepius comes to Athens
Thespis wins the first tragedy contest
Aristophanes’ Clouds
items.description: A comedy that makes fun of Socrates.

items.title: Herodotus’ Histories
items.description: The first long prose account of a war and the peoples in it.

items.title: City Dionysia
items.description: The spring festival where tragedies and comedies compete.

items.title: Cleisthenes
items.description: His reforms of 508 BCE founded Athenian democracy.

items.title: Pericles
items.description: The leading voice in Athens for thirty years.

items.title: Thucydides
items.description: General, exile and historian of the war.

items.title: Socrates
items.description: Asked questions in the marketplace until Athens had had enough.

items.title: Aristotle
items.description: Student of Plato, tutor of Alexander.

items.title: Alcibiades
items.description: Brilliant, vain and loyal to whoever was winning.

items.title: Demosthenes
items.description: Spent his career warning Athens about Philip.

notes.title: Why did Athens lose?
notes.body:
Thucydides blames the Sicilian Expedition more than anything. But the plague had already cost a quarter of the people, Decelea cut the farms off, and Aegospotami lost the last fleet.

It wasn’t one defeat. It was the money and the men running out.

notes.title: Where the fleet’s money came from
notes.body:
Silver from Laurion paid for the ships at Salamis. After 454 the league’s tribute paid for the Parthenon and for rowers.

So the same money explains the navy, the temple and the pay for jurors.

notes.title: Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Alexander
notes.body: Four generations of teacher and student. Socrates wrote nothing; Plato wrote him into dialogues; Aristotle left the Academy and tutored Alexander.

notes.title: How Greece lost its independence
notes.body: Demosthenes saw it coming. Chaeronea in 338 ended the argument, and the Lamian War in 322 was the last try.

notes.title: Sparta ran out of Spartans
notes.body: After Leuctra and the loss of Messenia, Sparta had few citizens and no helots to feed them.
